title: Electrical Safety on Site
whatItIs: Electricity gives no warning and can kill. Site tools and leads get rough use, so the lowest practical voltage, RCDs and checks before use keep you safe.

keyFacts.text: Electrical systems MUST be maintained, so far as reasonably practicable, to prevent danger.
Equipment made dead for work MUST be secured so it can't become live again during the work.
Anyone doing electrical work that needs technical knowledge MUST have it, or be properly supervised.

keyFacts: A 110 V supply centre-tapped to earth limits a shock to no more than 55 V to earth.
On 230 V, use an RCD that trips at 30 mA or less, and press its test button every day.
Check tool, lead and plug before use. Seen damage? Stop, report it and take it out of use.

visual.caption: Choose the lowest voltage that does the job (safest first)

items.title: Battery (cordless) tools
items.text: The safest choice. No extension leads or trailing cables.

items.title: 110 V reduced low voltage
items.text: Centre-tapped to earth, so at most 55 V to earth. Used for site power tools and lighting.

items.title: 230 V mains, only if needed
items.text: Only from RCD-protected sockets (30 mA or less). Best suited to dry indoor work.

a.label: Switching off
points: Someone else could switch it back on
Tape over a breaker is not acceptable

b.label: Isolating
points: Usually locked off at the isolator
Then proved dead before work starts

onTheTest.question: You need a power drill for work outdoors on a building site. Which option does HSE guidance say is the safest?
options: A 230 V drill on a household extension lead
A 230 V drill plugged into an adaptor
onTheTest.why: HSG141 para 36: battery-operated tools are the safest and remove the need for extension leads. 110 V systems can be used elsewhere.

onTheTest.question: The RCD on your 230 V supply keeps tripping. What should happen?
options: Bypass the RCD so work can carry on
Plug into a socket with no RCD
Stop and have the fault found by a competent person
Hold the reset button in while you work
onTheTest.why: HSG141 para 64: repeated tripping means something is likely wrong; a competent person should investigate. Never bypass or disable an RCD.

traps: Never accept being told equipment is dead. It must be proved dead first.
Tape over a circuit breaker is not a safe isolation: use a lock-off device.
Double-insulated tools are well protected, but their leads still get damaged.
An RCD helps, but it is not as safe as cordless tools or a 110 V supply.
